newsitem.title: USA: GAO says Pentagon made millions in overpayments. [CORRECTED 21:51 GMT]
newsitem.headline: GAO says Pentagon made millions in overpayments. [CORRECTED 21:51 GMT]

text.p: The Department of Defence has made hundreds of millions of dollars in overpayments to contractors because of its antiquated accounting and computer systems, a new report released Monday said.

The report by the General Accounting Office (GAO) did not attempt to tally all the overpayments, but focused on what was causing them -- computers that can't communicate with one another and the use of over 100 different accounting systems.

In addition, the Defence Department sometimes uses the same procedures to track purchases of a few dollars, like candies for a children's centre, as it does to check million-dollar weapons contracts, the report said.

"It is imperative that DOD (Department of Defence) achieve cost-effective control over its payment process," the report said. "Otherwise, it continues to risk hundreds of millions of dollars in potential overpayments."
Sen. Thomas Harkin of Iowa (corrects state from Missouri), who was one of the legislators who requested the report and released it to the news media, said the Pentagon had to take corrective action.
"The Pentagon's accounting system dates back to the Stone Age," Harkin said in a statement. "The DOD uses a magnifying glass to check tootsie roll purchase and misses the million dollar problems."

The report said the GAO had found that in one six-month period in fiscal year 1993, defence contractors returned $751 million in checks. When the GAO examined $392 million of these, it found that about $305 million represented overpayments by the government.

In one case, a contractor was overpaid $7.5 million, and the overpayment remained outstanding for eight years, the report said. By the time the government had figured out what happened, it had lost an estimated $5 million in interest.

The report said the Pentagon's non-integrated computer systems often requires personnel to make manual entry of data, leading to errors, and payments often require allocation among numerous accounting categories.
"Neither DOD nor the responsible contractors appeared to be aggressively pursuing resolution of payment discrepancies," it said.
The report said the Pentagon indicated it was already trying to improve its payment practices, but "DOD has a long way to go before its payment problems are under control."
